en: The *Saṃtati-vimokṣa-bhūmi-pāramitā-nītārtha-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of the Song Dynasty.
As stated in the *Saṃtati-vimokṣa-sūtra*: the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One!"

Bodhisattvas have ten stages, namely: the Stage of Joy, the Stage of Purity, the Stage of Illumination, the Stage of Blazing, the Stage Difficult to Conquer, the Stage of Presence, the Stage of Far-Going, the Immovable Stage, the Stage of Good Intelligence, and the Stage of the Dharma Cloud.
"Buddha-ground, the eleventh: by how many kinds of purification are these grounds subsumed, and how many divisions are there?
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva:
"There are four kinds of purification and eleven divisions that subsume these grounds."

Avalokiteśvara! The purity of aspiration encompasses the first stage; the purity of superior ethical discipline encompasses the second stage; the purity of superior mind encompasses the third stage; and the purity of superior wisdom—the supremely, most excellent purity—encompasses the fourth stage up to the Buddha stage. These four kinds of purity encompass those various stages.
"What are the eleven divisions?
Avalokiteśvara!
A Bodhisattva on the stage of practice through understanding has ten types of Dharma-practice: [text continues]"

Having well cultivated the bodhisattva’s liberation through patience and crossed over this stage, the bodhisattva ascends and transcends, fulfilling that portion of the state beyond birth; yet, he is not yet able to dwell in correct knowledge regarding subtle transgressions of the precepts, which constitutes an unfulfilled portion. To fulfill it, he applies skillful means and progresses until it is fulfilled.

He is not yet able to fully possess worldly samādhis and attainments, nor fulfill the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining, which constitutes an unfulfilled portion. To fulfill it, he applies skillful means and progresses until it is fulfilled.

He is not yet able to repeatedly cultivate the factors of enlightenment as they have been attained, nor is he yet able to relinquish attachment to the states of meditative attainment, which constitutes an unfulfilled portion. To fulfill it, he applies skillful means and progresses until it is fulfilled.

Yet, one has not yet been able to contemplate the ultimate truth; unable to abandon the one-sided intent that turns away from saṃsāra and heads toward nirvāṇa, one practices skillful means to gather and cultivate the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*). This portion is not yet fulfilled; for the sake of fulfillment, one seeks through skillful means until it is fully satisfied.

Furthermore, one has not yet been able to observe the arising of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) before one's eyes, but dwells frequently in revulsion and frequently in the signless (*animitta*).

This portion is not yet fulfilled; for the sake of fulfillment, one seeks through skillful means until it is fully satisfied. Furthermore, one has not yet been able to dwell frequently in uninterrupted, continuous, and signless contemplation. This portion is not yet fulfilled; for the sake of fulfillment, one seeks through skillful means until it is fully satisfied.

Yet, being unable to abandon the signless while still possessing activity and having attained the power of signs, this part is incomplete; for the sake of fulfillment, one applies skillful means to seek progress until it is fulfilled.

Being unable to ultimately discern all characteristics, discern all names, and attain mastery in teaching the Dharma in every way, this part is incomplete; for the sake of fulfillment, one applies skillful means to seek progress until it is fulfilled.
Being unable to receive and attain the fulfilled Dharmakāya, this part is incomplete; for the sake of fulfillment, one applies skillful means to seek progress until it is fulfilled.

Yet, being unable to attain unimpeded and unobstructed knowledge and vision regarding all objects of cognition (*jñeya*), this constitutes a partial lack of fulfillment; for the sake of fulfillment, one should apply skillful means to seek it further until fulfillment is attained.
Because those factors are fulfilled, all factors are fulfilled.
Avalokiteśvara!
These are called the four kinds of purity and the eleven factors that encompass all the stages (*bhūmi*).
Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason is the first stage called the Stage of Joy, and so on, up to the Buddha-stage which is called the Buddha-stage?”
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara:
"Because one ascends to the Great Meaning and attains the supreme, wondrous joy of the supramundane mind, the first stage is called the Stage of Joy."
Because it is free from all subtle transgressions of the precepts, the second stage is called the "Stainless Stage" (vimalā-bhūmi).
Because that samādhi and the retention of what has been heard rely upon the light of immeasurable wisdom, the third stage is called the "Luminous Stage" (prabhākari-bhūmi).
Because one burns away all afflictions with the flames of wisdom and cultivates the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), the fourth stage is called the "Blazing Stage" (*Arciṣmatī*).

Because one attains mastery through the arduous and diligent cultivation of those factors of enlightenment by means of skillful means (*upāya*), the fifth stage is called the "Difficult to Conquer Stage" (*Sudurjayā*).
Because one observes all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) directly and contemplates their manifold characteristics, the sixth stage is called the "Manifest" (*Abhimukhī*) stage.
Because one enters the distant [stages] and approaches the pure stages through uninterrupted and signless contemplation, the seventh stage is called the "Far-Reaching" (*Dūraṅgamā*) stage.

Because it is free from the characteristics of signs and the characteristics of mental development, and because afflictions neither arise nor move, the eighth stage is called the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*).

Because one attains vast wisdom that is faultless and possesses mastery over the teaching of the Dharma in all its aspects, the ninth stage is called the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*).
Because it pervasively covers all faults and evils, which are like space, with the Dharma-body that is like a great cloud, the tenth stage is called the *Dharmameghā-bhūmi* (Cloud of Dharma Stage).

Because one attains unimpeded and unobstructed cognition regarding all objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) and realizes the awakening to all aspects (*sarvākāra-abhisambodhi*), the eleventh stage is called the *Buddha-bhūmi*.
Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How many kinds of delusions and how many kinds of faults to be remedied are there in these stages?”
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara:
"There are twenty-two kinds of delusion and eleven kinds of faults to be remedied.
For beings on the first stage (*bhūmi*), there is the delusion of attachment to phenomena and the delusion of afflictions pertaining to the evil destinies; these are the faults to be remedied."
In the second bhūmi, there is the delusion regarding subtle transgressions of the precepts and the delusion regarding the various courses of karma; these are the faults to be remedied.
In the third bhūmi, there is the delusion regarding sensual desire and the delusion regarding the fulfillment of learning and retention; these are the faults to be remedied.
In the fourth stage, there is the delusion of craving for meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and the delusion of craving for the Dharma; these are the faults to be remedied.

In the fifth stage, there is the delusion of one-sided contemplation that turns away from saṃsāra and the delusion of one-sided contemplation that turns toward nirvāṇa; these are the faults to be remedied.

In the sixth stage, there is the delusion regarding the arising of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and the delusion regarding the multiplicity of their characteristics; these are the faults to be remedied.

In the seventh stage, there is the delusion regarding subtle characteristics and the delusion regarding the skillful means of one-pointed contemplation on the signless (*animitta*); these are the faults to be remedied.
In the eighth stage, there is the delusion regarding signlessness and non-development, and the delusion regarding mastery over signs; these are the faults to be remedied.

In the ninth stage, there is the delusion regarding mastery over the dhāraṇī of eloquence and the superior wisdom that delights in explaining immeasurable teachings through immeasurable words and phrases, as well as the delusion regarding mastery over eloquence itself; these are the faults to be remedied.
In the tenth stage, there is the delusion regarding great supernormal powers and the delusion regarding entry into subtle secrets; these are the faults to be remedied.

In the Buddha-stage, there is the delusion regarding all objective spheres (*jñeya*) and subtle meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), and the delusion regarding obstructions; these are the faults to be remedied.
Avalokiteśvara!
These are called the twenty-two forms of folly and the eleven kinds of faults to be remedied.
They are established within those various stages and are not in accord with unsurpassed bodhi.
Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How marvelous, World-Honored One!
Supreme Bodhi is of great benefit and great fruit; those bodhisattvas have torn through the great net of delusion and crossed over great transgressions to attain supreme Bodhi.”
Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
In these various stages, how many kinds of excellence are established?"
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara:

“There are eight matters, namely: purity of aspiration, purity of mind, purity of compassion, purity of the pāramitās, purity of seeing and making offerings to the Buddhas, purity of maturing sentient beings, purity of birth, and purity of power.”
Avalokiteśvara!

From the first stage (*bhūmi*), there is an increase in the purity of aspiration, up to the purity of power; likewise, from the progressively higher stages up to the Buddha-stage (*buddhabhūmi*), there is an increase in the purity of aspiration, up to the purity of power. One should know that these constitute purity. Within that Buddha-stage, with the sole exception of the purity of birth, one should know that the merits of those stages—from the first stage up to the highest stage—are each increasingly superior within their respective stages.
"All the stages of the bodhisattvas possess superior merits; only the merits of the stage of the Tathāgata are unsurpassed.
Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"For what reason is the Bodhisattva supreme among all those born?
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara: "There are four reasons:

namely, because they have gathered fast, pure, and wholesome roots; because they take up [the path] according to wisdom; because they rescue all sentient beings through compassion; and because they themselves are free from defilement and cause others to be free from it as well."
Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason do bodhisattvas give rise to wondrous vows, supreme vows, and vows of renowned power?”
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara:

"There are four matters by which that bodhisattva skillfully dwells in the bliss of nirvāṇa and is capable of swiftly attaining it; and by swiftly abandoning [samsāra] and dwelling in bliss, without cause and without purpose, he makes a vow for the sake of sentient beings who have long endured manifold sufferings. Therefore, this sublime vow, this supreme vow, is called the 'Vow of Power'."
Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How many matters are there for a bodhisattva to study?”
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara:
"There are six matters in which a bodhisattva trains, namely the six pāramitās: from dānapāramitā up to prajñāpāramitā."
Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Of these six matters of training, how many pertain to the training in higher ethical discipline (adhiśīla-śikṣā), how many to the training in higher mind (adhicitta-śikṣā), and how many to the training in higher wisdom (adhiprajñā-śikṣā)?”
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara:

“Generosity, ethical discipline, and patience—these three constitute the training in higher ethics; meditative concentration is the training in higher mind; and wisdom is the training in higher wisdom;
diligence pervades them all.”
Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Of these six matters, how many are the requisites for merit, and how many are the requisites for wisdom?”
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara:
"The training in higher ethical discipline is the equipment for merit; the training in higher wisdom is the equipment for insight; meditation and diligence pertain to both."
Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, how should a bodhisattva train in these six matters of study?
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara:

“There are five things associated with the pāramitās: namely, having supreme faith and understanding in the Bodhisattva-piṭaka which teaches the true Dharma; performing the ten dharma-practices therein; protecting the bodhicitta through the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation; associating with spiritual friends; and practicing wholesome deeds continuously through skillful means.”
Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason are these various matters of training established in six categories?”
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara:
"There are two matters: first, the gathering of sentient beings; second, the counteracting of afflictions.
Those three trainings gather sentient beings, and those three trainings counteract afflictions."
The Bodhisattva gathers in sentient beings by providing them with various requisites through the practice of giving;
the Bodhisattva gathers in sentient beings by benefiting them with fearlessness through the observance of ethical discipline, neither causing harm nor intimidation;
the Bodhisattva gathers in sentient beings by enduring harm, oppression, and terror through the practice of patience.
By means of these three trainings, one gathers in sentient beings.

Through diligent vigor, one subdues the afflictions; by giving rise to the cultivation and study of wholesome deeds that sever the afflictions, one studies and practices wholesome deeds without being moved by any afflictions;
and through meditative concentration, one suppresses the afflictions.
"One cuts off all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) through wisdom;
by means of these three trainings, one counteracts the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason are the other four pāramitās established?
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara:
"Because these are the companions of the six pāramitās.

Those three pāramitās embrace sentient beings; they are established through the bodhisattva’s skillful means of the bases of sympathy (saṃgrahavastu). Therefore, I say that the pāramitā of skillful means is the companion of those three pāramitās."
Furthermore, Avalokiteśvara!

When a bodhisattva, in the present life, frequently engages in afflictions and is unable to endure the constant cultivation of patience; because they crave and delight in the lower realms, their aspirations are weak and inferior, and they cannot unify the mind within; and because, despite hearing and practicing based on the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, they cannot open up and draw forth supramundane wisdom, yet they practice with meager merit and vow that in future lives their afflictions will be thin and slight—this is the perfection of aspiration (praṇidhāna-pāramitā).
Once the afflictions have been thinned, one is able to apply diligent effort; therefore, I say that the *praṇidhāna-pāramitā* is the companion of the *vīrya-pāramitā*.

By associating with spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), hearing the sublime Dharma, and engaging in correct internal reflection, one transforms inferior aspirations into the attainment of power and aspirations, and becomes capable of one-pointed concentration within the superior realms; therefore, I say that the *bala-pāramitā* is the companion of the *dhyāna-pāramitā*.

To hear and cultivate meditation based on the Bodhisattva-piṭaka is the perfection of wisdom (*jñāna-pāramitā*); it is capable of opening up and drawing forth supramundane insight. Therefore, I say that the perfection of wisdom is the companion of the perfection of insight (*prajñā-pāramitā*).
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
for what reason are the six pāramitās taught in such a sequence?”
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara:
“Because they rely on that supreme attraction, bodhisattvas relinquish body and wealth to uphold the pure precepts;

because they protect the precepts, they practice patience; having practiced patience, they apply diligence; having applied diligence, they are able to cultivate dhyāna; and once dhyāna is perfected, they attain supramundane wisdom.”
Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How many kinds of distinctions are there among those various pāramitās?"
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara:
"Each has three types.
As for the three types of dānapāramitā, they are the giving of Dharma, the giving of material wealth, and the giving of fearlessness."
The three types of *śīlapāramitā* are: the precept of relinquishing unwholesome conduct, the precept of generating wholesome conduct, and the precept of benefiting sentient beings.
The three types of *kṣāntipāramitā* are: patience toward harm, patience in enduring suffering, and patience in contemplating the Dharma.
The three types of *vīrya-pāramitā* (perfection of vigor) are: the vigor of great vows, the vigor of skillful means, and the vigor of benefiting sentient beings.

The three types of *dhyāna-pāramitā* (perfection of meditation) are: the meditation of dwelling in the bliss of counteracting the suffering of afflictions through the stillness that is free from false conceptualization; the meditation that draws forth meritorious qualities; and the meditation that draws forth the benefit of sentient beings.
"The three kinds of Prajñāpāramitā are: the condition of worldly truth, the condition of ultimate truth, and the condition of benefiting sentient beings.
Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One!"
"For what reason are these pāramitās called 'pāramitās'?
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara:
"There are five kinds: first, non-obstruction; second, lack of concern; third, absence of fault; fourth, absence of false conceptualization; and fifth, dedication."
"Unobstructed" means being unstained by things contrary to the perfections;
"unregarding" means having a mind that is not bound to the karmic rewards of the perfections or to worldly benefits;
and "faultless" means, regarding the various perfections, being free from defiled and unskillful methods.
"Absence of conceptual construction" means not adhering to the specific characteristics of the various *pāramitās* as they are expressed in words;
"dedication" means that these *pāramitās*, having been performed and cultivated, are directed toward the attainment of the fruit of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what constitutes an act contrary to the pāramitās?”
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara:
"You should know that there are six matters: first, desiring wealth and prosperity, one regards oneself as a sovereign lord, perceiving personal security, merit, and benefit;
second, acting according to one's desires with body, speech, and mind."
Third, being unable to endure a mind of contempt toward others;
fourth, not diligently applying skillful means toward all wholesome dharmas;
fifth, habitually associating with and becoming familiar with the various worldly affairs that are perceived, heard, sensed, and cognized.
"Sixth, there is the view that worldly frivolous discourse produces merit.
Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What are the fruits and rewards of these pāramitās?

The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara: "They also have six kinds: first, great wealth; second, rebirth in the happy realms; third, being without enemies; fourth, being indestructible; fifth, being a sovereign lord over many joyful beings; and sixth, not harming oneself while possessing great capability."
Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What defiled dharmas are mixed with these pāramitās?”
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara: "You should know that there are four kinds:
first, the skillful means lacking compassion; second, the skillful means of improper reflection; third, the skillful means that are not constant; and fourth, the skillful means that are not sudden."
"One who employs improper reflection as a skillful means practices these perfections in a manner that is confused with other perfections.
Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
“What, then, is not skillful means?
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara:
“Having already cultivated these various pāramitās and gathered in sentient beings, one feels joy in the mind when benefiting them with even a small amount of material wealth.”
To not cause sentient beings to awaken to what is unwholesome and instead establish them in states of wholesomeness is called a non-expedient means.
Why is this so? Because this does not constitute a Bodhisattva’s benefit for sentient beings.
Just as with impure substances, whether they be many or few, there is no skillful means by which one can make them fragrant;

likewise, for sentient beings whose nature is suffering due to these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), small benefits or favors cannot bring them peace and happiness. Only the supreme gathering [of beings] establishes them in the state of goodness.
Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How many kinds of purity are there for these pāramitās?”
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara:
"I do not say that these pāramitās have a purity apart from those five kinds; rather, today I shall analyze them both collectively and individually according to those very matters."
To state it in summary, one should know that the purification of all *pāramitās* consists of seven aspects.

What are these seven? They are: when a bodhisattva does not seek to have others know of this dharma; does not cling to this dharma; sees no doubt or confusion regarding this vehicle of the Bodhi-dharma; neither exalts himself nor disparages others as to whether something is right or wrong; is neither arrogant nor negligent; does not give rise to the thought of contentment through meager or inferior means; and does not give rise to a mind of stinginess or envy toward this dharma.
Now, the purity of the *pāramitās* shall be explained according to their specific characteristics; one should know that there are seven kinds. What are these seven?

They refer to the seven kinds of pure giving (*śuddha-dāna*) that a bodhisattva upholds and practices as taught by me: namely, the purity of the gift itself, the purity of ethical discipline, the purity of view, the purity of mind, the purity of speech, the purity of wisdom, and the purity of defilement-free giving. These seven are called the purity of the *dānapāramitā*.

It refers to the bodhisattva’s skillful mastery of all forms of the restraint of the precepts (*śīla-saṃvara*), skill in the precepts for emerging from transgressions, the precepts of constancy, the precepts of firmness, the precepts of constant practice, the precepts of constant application, and the precepts of formal training; these seven kinds are called the purification of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).

That is to say, a bodhisattva relies on their own karmic retribution; regarding all harmful matters, their mind harbors no resentment. Whether they are reviled, provoked to anger, struck, or contested, they do not retaliate against any such harm.

To harbor no resentment toward enemies or those one dislikes; to accept their apologies sincerely and without obstruction when they seek reconciliation; not to expect an apology when others offend one; to accept such offenses with compassion according to the Dharma, remaining fearless and free from seeking recompense; and to constantly act for the benefit of others without ever abandoning them—these seven aspects are called the purification of the *kṣānti-pāramitā*.

This refers to the Bodhisattva’s skillful knowledge of equanimous diligence (*samatā-vīrya*), not exalting oneself or disparaging others on account of such diligence, and being single-mindedly devoted to all wholesome dharmas through diligence, capability, firmness, and non-abandonment; these seven aspects are called the purification of the *vīryapāramitā*.

It refers to the bodhisattva’s skillful entry into the samādhi-dhyāna of signlessness, the samādhi-dhyāna of fulfillment, the samādhi-dhyāna conjoined with ethical discipline, the great samādhi-dhyāna, the samādhi-dhyāna of non-reliance, the samādhi-dhyāna of skillful cultivation, and the immeasurable samādhi-dhyānas cultivated through hearing and reflecting upon the Bodhisattvapiṭaka; these seven kinds are called the purity of the dhyāna-pāramitā.

This means that when a bodhisattva abandons both the establishment [of extremes] and their denial, the wisdom of the Middle Way emerges; by means of that wisdom, they understand the meaning of the gates of liberation as they truly are.
One understands, as they truly are, the meaning of the intrinsic nature of the three gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
One also understands, as they truly are, the meaning of the absence of intrinsic nature in these three types of intrinsic nature: whether they be the imagined, the dependent, or the perfected.

Whether it be characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), or the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), one understands these three types as being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and according to the meaning of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) as they truly are.
One also understands the meaning of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) within the five fields of knowledge (*pañca-vidyā-sthāna*) as it truly is.

Abiding extensively in the seven kinds of suchness, free from conceptual construction and devoid of hypocrisy, one gives rise to the contemplation of the objects of the lower stages through a single gateway; these seven kinds of "progressing toward the Dharma according to the Dharma" are called the purification of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What are the respective karmas of those five types?”
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara:
"You should know that there are five activities.
For a Bodhisattva who is unimpeded, these consist of the constant and simultaneous application of skillful means and heedfulness regarding the perfections in the present life."
Being without concern means embracing the causes of heedfulness for the future.
Being without fault means cultivating and perfecting the pure pāramitās.
Being without conceptual construction means that through skillful means, one swiftly fulfills the pāramitās.

Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) means that in all births one constantly attains the inexhaustible perfection (*pāramitā*) of receiving the fruits of wholesome karma, up until the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Among these various pāramitās, which is the most supreme?”
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara:
"It refers to being unimpeded, without regard, and dedicated [to awakening].
What is non-defilement?"
"It means being without fault and without conceptual construction. "What is 'blazing'?
"It means not calculating by number."
"What is immovability?
"It refers to entering the stage of the dharma of non-retrogression.
"What is swift purity?"
"It means to dwell in the ten stages while seeking the stage of Buddhahood.
Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"For what reason does a bodhisattva always obtain the fruition of inexhaustible pāramitās and possess inexhaustible pāramitās?
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara:
"Because they are mutually dependent and because they are practiced through relinquishment."
Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
for what reason do Bodhisattvas deeply delight in the pāramitās and receive their karmic retribution?”
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara: “A bodhisattva has five matters:

first, the true cause for the superior joy and bliss of the various pāramitās; second, the cause for gathering and benefiting oneself and others; third, the cause for receiving retribution in future lives; fourth, the removal of afflictions; and fifth, not dwelling in the evil destinies.”
Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What specific virtues and powers do each of these pāramitās possess?”
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara:

“You should know that there are four kinds in each case: first, when a bodhisattva cultivates the various pāramitās, they abandon stinginess, greed, violation of precepts, indolence, distracted mind, and various views;
second, these serve as the true requisites for unsurpassed bodhi.”
"Third, one gathers benefit for oneself and others within the present life;
fourth, one shall obtain vast and inexhaustible fruits of retribution in future lives.
Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What are the causes and what are the fruits of these pāramitās?”
"What is their meaning?
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara:
"These pāramitās have compassion as their cause; taking in and gathering sentient beings through the reception of retribution is their fruit; and fulfilling great bodhi is their great purpose."
Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there are bodhisattvas who possess inexhaustible wealth and a heart of compassion, for what reason are there impoverished sentient beings in the world?”
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara:
"This is merely the fault of the karmic deeds of sentient beings themselves.
If it were otherwise, others would constantly provide for them, and they would possess inexhaustible wealth; how then could there be impoverished sentient beings in the world?"
If that were so, the evil deeds committed by sentient beings would not constitute an obstacle.
Avalokiteśvara!
It is like a hungry ghost, driven by thirst, who sees only empty ravines.
It is not the fault of that ocean, but merely the fault of the karmic actions of those hungry ghosts themselves.
Just as that great ocean is without fault, so too is the Bodhisattva without fault;
just as it is the fruit of the hungry ghosts' own karma, so too is the karmic retribution of sentient beings.
Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since all dharmas are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature, by means of which pāramitā does a bodhisattva take them up?”
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara:
“Prajñāpāramitā. Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If the Prajñāpāramitā grasps that which lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), why does it not grasp that which possesses intrinsic nature?
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara:

“I do not say that one apprehends the absence of intrinsic nature by means of the absence of intrinsic nature; rather, the absence of intrinsic nature is known through its own nature beyond words. Since it cannot be explained apart from words, one apprehends the absence of intrinsic nature by means of departing from [the notion of] intrinsic nature.”
Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding the pāramitās you have spoken of—the supreme pāramitā and the great pāramitā—what constitutes a pāramitā, what constitutes a supreme pāramitā, and what constitutes a great pāramitā?”
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva:

"Having cultivated and perfected wholesome dharmas such as *dāna* over immeasurable periods of time, one is able to subdue the active afflictions (*kleśa*) and is not overcome by them; this refers to the transformation of the soft and medium levels of understanding on the stage of practice through liberation (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), which is called a *pāramitā*."

Furthermore, having cultivated such wholesome dharmas as these for immeasurable periods until they are perfected, one is able to sever the afflictions even while they are active; thus, one is not overcome by them. This is called the "superior pāramitā" arising from the first bhūmi.

Furthermore, after practicing such wholesome dharmas for immeasurable periods until they are perfected, all afflictions cease to function at all; this is said to arise in the eighth stage and is called the Great Pāramitā.
Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How many kinds of afflictions and latent tendencies (anuśaya) are there in these stages?”
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara:
“There are three kinds. The first is ‘harming one’s companions,’ which refers to the fifth stage.
Avalokiteśvara!”
The activity of non-coemergent afflictions lacks its companion—the activity of coemergent afflictions—at that time; therefore, it is called "the destruction of the companion.

Second is "the weakening of the latent tendencies" (*anuśaya*), which refers to the subtle activities of the sixth and seventh stages being suppressed and rendered inactive through the practice of *śamatha* (calm abiding).

Third is the subtle latent tendency (*anuśaya*), which refers to the eighth stage (*bhūmi*); because all superior and superior afflictions (*kleśa*) do not function therein, and because the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) rely only slightly upon it.
Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How many kinds of faults must a bodhisattva sever to be said to have severed those underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*)?”
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara:
"There are three kinds: first, the severance of the fault of the skin; second, the severance of the fault of the flesh; and third, the severance of the fault of the bone.
To be free from all messengers—this, I say, is the stage of the Buddha alone."
Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Through how many asaṃkhyeya kalpas does a bodhisattva sever those various faults?”
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara: "There are three immeasurable units:

the *kṣaṇa*, the *lava*, and the *muhūrta*; the half-period (*ardha-yāma*), the period (*yāma*), the day and night; the half-month and the month; and three months (according to the Danxiang edition, two) constitute one season (*ṛtu*); one season is called a *ṛtu*."
Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When afflictions arise in these bodhisattvas of the various stages, what are their characteristics, what are their faults, and what are their virtues?”
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara:
"It is the characteristic of being unstained. Why is this so?

This means that when a bodhisattva enters the entire dharma-realm in the first stage, they know the arising of afflictions; it is not that they do not know them. Therefore, this is called the characteristic of non-defilement.

Because they do not cause suffering to arise within themselves, there is no fault; rather, because they act as the cause for the realm of sentient beings to become free from suffering, the afflictions that bodhisattvas give rise to possess immeasurable merit.
Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How marvelous, World-Honored One!

Even the Great Meaning of Bodhi causes afflictions to arise in bodhisattvas, yet it surpasses the roots of goodness and meritorious virtues of all sentient beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas—how much more so other virtues!”
Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding what the World-Honored One has taught—that the Śrāvaka Vehicle and the Mahāyāna are in fact the Single Vehicle—what is the meaning of this?”
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara:

"When I speak of the Śrāvaka vehicle, that is to say, the five aggregates, the six internal sense bases, and the six external sense bases—such as these, I declare, are themselves the Mahāyāna, the single Dharma-realm, and the single path. Therefore, I do not say that there are various vehicles."

Yet, based on the meaning as it was thus explained, they give rise to false imaginings, either establishing or denigrating various vehicles; because their views conflict and they engage in mutual disputes, they speak in this manner.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The various natures that are taught Are all of one and the same path;
Whether inferior or sublime vehicles, There is no difference between them."
As it is said: "Following after conceptual construction, one either establishes [existence] or denies [it];
those views contradict the true meaning, as the deluded have various understandings.
The stages (bhūmi) are comprised of the objects of thought to be remedied, the superior births, and the training in vows."
"This explains the path of the Mahāyāna; by diligent cultivation, one swiftly attains Buddhahood.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"In the *Saṃtati-vimokṣa-sūtra*, what is the name of this sutra,
and how should it be upheld?
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara:
"This sutra is titled 'The Definitive Exposition of the Grounds and Perfections'; thus should it be upheld.
When this definitive exposition of the grounds and perfections was spoken, seventy-five thousand bodhisattvas attained the Mahāyāna-light Samādhi.
